titulo.texto: Mural “Con pasión por los mayas,” by Rina Lazo

frase_gancho.texto: A Guatemalan painter who copied Bonampak and painted for this museum.

puente_narrativo.texto: With this mural, the Maya world ends and we enter the Western Mexico hall. It begins with one of its oldest pieces: a gray vessel with a stirrup-shaped handle.

guion_corto.texto: Rina Lazo was born in Guatemala in 1923 and came to Mexico in 1947 on a scholarship to study painting. Here she became an assistant to Diego Rivera and grew into one of the last great muralists of the country. Her life remained tied to the Maya world. You have already seen the copies of the Bonampak murals, which she painted for this very museum. Besides that feat in the outdoor garden, Rina Lazo created for the museum the portable mural “Venerable Abuelo Maíz” (also known in the museum’s exhibitions as “Con pasión por los mayas”). The title says a great deal about her: for decades she painted the Maya with admiration. Look at this work with the Bonampak copies in mind. One is a faithful replica of an ancient original. The other is the personal vision of a twentieth-century artist.

guion_largo.texto:
If you walked through the [Bonampak temple](mna_s09_templo_bonampak), you already know Rina Lazo’s hand. This mural is another work of hers, and behind it lies a life worth telling.

Rina Lazo was born in Guatemala in 1923. In 1947 she came to Mexico on a scholarship and entered La Esmeralda, the school of painting, sculpture, and engraving. A few months later she was already working on Diego Rivera’s team. Her first collaboration was “Sueño de una tarde dominical en la Alameda Central.” Later she helped with the Cárcamo del río Lerma, in Chapultepec, and with the mosaics of the stadium at Ciudad Universitaria. She used to say that her true school had been Rivera’s workshop.

The museum gave her a task very different from painting a mural of her own: copying. In 1964, the architect Pedro Ramírez Vázquez commissioned from her a replica of the Maya paintings of Bonampak. It was made for the museum’s opening in 1964. It is said that she traveled to the jungle of Chiapas to copy the figures one by one, before time went on erasing them.

The Maya were her theme throughout her life. As early as 1954 she had painted “Tierra fértil,” her first fresco, with memories of Tikal and of the fertility of the Guatemalan land. She donated it to a museum of the University of San Carlos, in her country. In 1997 she painted “Realidad y sueño en el mundo maya” together with her husband, the painter Arturo García Bustos. He also painted for this museum, and later on you will see his work in the ethnography halls.

Now, the work in front of you. The Gaceta de Museos del INAH mentions it as “Con pasión por los mayas,” among the large-format paintings that have come to the museum. What scenes it contains is something you will discover by looking at it. The title speaks of passion, and her life confirms it: from “Tierra fértil,” in 1954, to “Xibalbá,” her last great work, more than sixty years of painting the Maya went by.

There is also another work of hers often cited for this hall, “Venerable abuelo maíz.” It is described as a great canvas of more than nineteen meters. Its scenes are inspired by the Popol Vuh, the sacred book of the Maya, such as the creation of people. It is not certain whether this is the same painting under another title or a different work. The museum’s wall label will clarify it.

In her last years she worked on “Xibalbá, el inframundo de los mayas,” a mural inspired by the caves of Cobán, in Guatemala. It was exhibited at the Palacio de Bellas Artes in 2022. Lazo died in November 2019, at the age of ninety-six. Xibalbá is the underworld of the Popol Vuh. There the twins played ball with the lords of death, as you saw on the [Chinkultic marker](mna_s09_disco_chinkultic).

A painter born in Guatemala was, for more than half a century, one of the most constant voices of Maya art in Mexico. Before moving on, compare the colors of this mural with the blue of Bonampak. They are two works by the same hand, and one and the same affection for a people that is still alive.

texto.Author: Rina Lazo (1923-2019)
texto.Works at the MNA: Fresco replica of the Bonampak murals (1964) and tempera mural on linen “Venerable Abuelo Maíz / Con pasión por los mayas” (1995-1996, 2.70 x 19.00 m)

texto.pregunta: Myth: The Bonampak paintings seen in the museum are the originals.
texto.respuesta: Reality: They are copies made by Rina Lazo. The originals remain on the walls of the temple, in the jungle of Chiapas.
